persona.who: 66, retired bank officer in Lucknow, wife passed 2 years ago, son in Toronto, daughter in Mumbai. Reads the Gita occasionally, wants to understand it properly.
persona.note: after my wife left us the house is very quiet. children call on sunday. I have time now and I want to read Gita properly not just the shlokas everyone forwards on whatsapp

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call searching for what it's all for, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the search as your own, and the quiet as the space where it can begin.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the self that does not pass is the one you are seeking.
week_beats.act: You try reading one chapter with attention to the one question that speaks to you, and let the rest wait.
week_beats.story: A king who lost everything and found that the self was the answer shows you what seeking can become.

queries.hook: The search for something deeper in a quiet house, where the verses that come on WhatsApp are not enough.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: The self that does not pass is the one you are seeking; it was always there, and it does not leave.
queries.act: Read one chapter with attention to the one question that speaks to you today, and let the rest wait.
queries.story: A king who lost everything and sat in the quiet forest, seeking what does not pass, and found that the self was the answer.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् । अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
verse.line: Even winning everything wouldn't touch this grief that's drying me up inside.
verse.translation: I see nothing that could drive away this sorrow that is drying up my senses, not even an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom on earth or rule over the gods.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands on the field of battle, his body heavy and his mind empty. He tells Krishna that even if he were to take every kingdom and rule the gods, none of it would touch the grief that has taken hold of him. He says he sees nothing that can drive this sorrow away, nothing at all. This is the moment he admits he does not know the way forward and asks to be taught.
verse.for_you: The house is very quiet now. You have the time for this search. You are not looking for a cure. You are looking for what it is all for. That is a clear place to stand. You can begin from there.

verse.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
verse.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
verse.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
verse.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
verse.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

verse.meaning: A teacher speaks of a hidden gold buried under the ground. People walk over it every day and never see it. They are carried away by what is not true. This is what happens to us. We pass our own deepest self every night in sleep without knowing it. The verse proposes that your treasure is already here, but you walk past it because you are following what is false. The next step is to stop walking past it and to look for what is real.
verse.for_you: Your house is quiet. Your children call on Sundays. You feel this life has a hidden gold you walk over each day without knowing. Let the Gita be the map. Look for what is real in the silence, not what is false.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse.sanskrit: देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा । तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥
verse.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.
verse.why: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

prasang.title: The teaching of the deathless Self (Sankhya)
prasang.summary: Krishna begins his teaching: the self is eternal, bodies change like clothes, and pleasure and pain come and go. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
prasang.lesson: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that the soul is eternal and cannot be cut, burned, wetted, or dried. He says that the soul is unborn, eternal, and unchanging. He tells Arjuna that he should not grieve for the soul, for it is eternal and cannot be destroyed.
verse.for_you: The self that does not pass is the one you are seeking. Hold onto that while the grief moves through you, knowing it does not define what remains.

verse.speaker: Sage Nishakara
verse.setting: The old vulture Sampati, wings burnt and grounded for ages, is told why he should live on.
verse.sanskrit: उत्सहेयमहं कर्तुमद्यैव त्वां सपक्षकम्। इहस्थस्त्वं हि लोकानां हितं कार्यं करिष्यसि॥
verse.line: You are needed exactly where you are, as you are. Your use isn't over.
verse.translation: I could give you back your wings this very day. But by staying here as you are, you will do something for the good of the world.
verse.why: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

prasang.title: Sampati, the bird who could not fly
prasang.summary: The despairing monkeys meet Sampati, Jatayu's old brother, whose wings burnt long ago. A sage once told him to live on, because one day his knowledge would be needed. Now he tells them Sita is in Lanka, and his wings grow back.
prasang.story_hook: For thousands of years the old bird had sat on a mountain with no wings, waiting for a reason.
prasang.lesson: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

verse.meaning: Sage Nishakara tells the old vulture Sampati that even now, in his grounded state, he is needed. The sage could restore his wings, but Sampati is asked to stay exactly as he is. This is because his long years of sitting with his loss have given him a sight the others lack. He knows where Sita is. By holding his place without running from it, he serves the world. The verse asks you to trust that your own stillness now is not empty. It is a place of seeing.
verse.for_you: The quiet house feels like a loss of use. But this stillness is where you meet your own question. Let the house hold you. You do not need to fix the silence today. You only need to stay in it and see what it shows you.

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: A seer is speaking to someone who is listening. They have been told to enjoy what is around them by letting go. Now they are told to do their work and wish for a full hundred years. This is the only way to live. If you do your work with this spirit, your actions will not cling to you or weigh you down. You keep what you have lightly, you keep working, and you see yourself in everyone else.
verse.for_you: You have time now, and you are reading the Gita. Read one chapter today and notice the one question that speaks to you. Let the rest wait. Your use is not over. Your part is to read with attention.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna begins his ladder of practices with the simplest instruction.
verse.sanskrit: मय्येव मन आधत्स्व मयि बुद्धिं निवेशय । निवसिष्यसि मय्येव अत ऊर्ध्वं न संशयः ॥
verse.line: Rest your mind in me, settle your thinking in me, and you will live in me.
verse.translation: Fix your mind on me alone, let your understanding settle in me; from then on you will dwell in me. Of this there is no doubt.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is offering a ladder of practices, and he begins with the simplest rung. He tells Arjuna to rest his mind in him and let his understanding settle there. From that settled place, Arjuna will live in him. The verse proposes that when your thinking stops moving and settles on one thing, you begin to truly dwell within it. It is a shift from scattered effort to a single, steady focus.
verse.for_you: The house is quiet enough for your mind to settle. With your children's calls and your reading, let your attention rest on one question from the first chapter. Let the rest wait.

story.title: Rama comes home from his pilgrimage and loses interest in everything
story.story_hook: The prince who had everything came back from his travels and stopped laughing.
story.summary: Sixteen-year-old Rama returns from a long pilgrimage and quietly withdraws: he stops eating properly, stops laughing, ignores his duties and sits alone. His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.
story.lesson: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

anchor.speaker: Rama's attendant
anchor.setting: Rama's attendants tell King Dasharatha how the prince has changed since his pilgrimage.
anchor.sanskrit: रामो राजीवपत्राक्षो यतःप्रभृति चागतः । सविप्रस्तीर्थयात्रायास्ततःप्रभृति दुर्मनाः ॥
anchor.line: Ever since he came back from the trip, he hasn't been himself.
anchor.translation: Ever since lotus-eyed Rama came back from his pilgrimage with the brahmins, he has been low in spirit.
anchor.why: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

script: The house is very quiet now. You have the time for this search. You are not looking for a cure. You are looking for what it is all for. That is a clear place to stand. You can begin from there.

Arjuna stands on the field of battle, his body heavy and his mind empty. He tells Krishna that even if he were to take every kingdom and rule the gods, none of it would touch the grief that has taken hold of him. He says he sees nothing that can drive this sorrow away, nothing at all. This is the moment he admits he does not know the way forward and asks to be taught. Arjuna said:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम्, अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम्.
In plain words: Even winning everything wouldn't touch this grief that's drying me up inside.

Admitting you do not know is not a failure. It is the only honest ground to stand on when everything you once believed in has faded. This is easier said than done, because the mind wants to find a quick answer and move past the pain. But here, there is no quick answer. There is only the quiet admission that the old reasons no longer hold, and the courage to ask for help in the dark.
Let the quiet house hold your confusion without rushing to fix it. When you sit down to read, let the words land without needing to understand them all at once. Let the search be enough for today.
What would it be like to simply say I do not know?

depth.life: The house is very quiet. Your children call on Sundays. You sit with time you did not plan for, and you want to read the Gita with your own eyes, not just forwarded verses. You are quietly grieving, and you feel lost in what is left.
depth.points: Arjuna, a warrior, sees every possible prize and says none of it touches the grief inside him. He admits he does not know what to do. The truth underneath is that clarity begins only when we stop pretending we know the answer and ask for help.
depth.practice: Open your Gita to any chapter. Read one verse slowly. Then write down the one question it leaves in you.
depth.question: What is the one thing you truly want to understand?
